paras: The lynching of Hamilton Staples was the killing of a Black man near Atlanta, Texas, reported as having taken place on July 11, 1888. According to a syndicated news digest, Staples was lynched after being accused of assaulting the seventeen-year-old daughter of Hardy McCoy, described as a wealthy planter. The episode is known only from that one sentence, which several Midwestern weeklies printed in the following days.

The digest stated that "Hamilton Staples (colored) was lynched on the 11th near Atlanta, Tex.," giving the alleged assault as the reason. It did not say who carried out the lynching, how many took part, whether Staples had been arrested beforehand, or how he was killed. The accusation itself appeared only as the digest's wording, with no account of the alleged assault or of any investigation.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The item reached readers through a ready-made weekly news digest rather than a local Texas report. The Mower County Transcript of Lansing, Minnesota, ran it on July 18, 1888, the Kanabec County Times of Mora, Minnesota, on July 19, and the Griggs Courier of Cooperstown, Dakota Territory, on July 20, each word for word. In each paper the sentence sat in a column headed "DOMESTIC" between notices of a stable fire in Wichita and a woman burned to death in Louisville, with no headline or comment of its own.

The wording presented the accusation as the cause of the killing ("for assaulting") and identified Staples by race with the parenthetical "colored," while naming the alleged victim only through her father's standing as "a wealthy planter."

reader.title: Lynching of Hamilton Staples
bases: The digest item says Hamilton Staples was 'lynched' near Atlanta, Tex., over an alleged assault (A1).

The only report says Staples was 'lynched' for an alleged assault, which states a killing outside the law under a pretext of punishing a crime (A1); it gives no detail of the mob, its size or the method, so the group element rests on the word 'lynched' alone.
All three printings carry the identical sentence from one syndicated news digest, so they are one report, not independent confirmation (A1, A2, A3).

framing.detail: Midwestern weeklies ran the item as one undifferentiated sentence in a 'DOMESTIC' digest, stating the alleged assault as the reason ('for assaulting') without comment.

record_check.dossier: The item says the lynching took place 'on the 11th'; 1888-07-18 is the issue date of the first printing. The event date is July 11, 1888.
No county is named; the coverage says only 'near Atlanta, Tex.' Cass is an inference from the town, not a reported fact.
Lynched on the 11th, not the 18th; the assault is an accusation, not an established fact.
The same digest sentence ran in at least three papers, July 18-20, 1888.
